slides.title: Basis Blades and Operations
slides.notes: Open by lowering the abstraction level deliberately. The lecture is not about a new geometric model; it is about the tiny representation contract that every later product depends on. The key promise is that a blade address, a sign rule, and a metric rule are enough to build reliable sparse multivector operations.

slides.title: Blade Addresses
slides.notes: Emphasize that the bitmap is an address, not a visual drawing of the blade. Bit zero names e1 even though it prints on the right side of a binary string. Once that convention is accepted, grade counting, table indexing, and dependency tests become ordinary integer operations.

slides.title: Bit Tests Become Algebra Tests
slides.notes: Use the three bit operations as the computational vocabulary for the chapter. Popcount reads grade, bitwise and detects shared basis-vector factors, and exclusive-or gives the canonical output address after common factors are removed. The arithmetic looks small because the convention has already stored the algebraic ordering.

slides.title: Swap Parity Gives The Sign
slides.notes: Slow down here because sign bugs are contagious. Concatenate the left blade factors with the right blade factors, then count how many inversions must be swapped to restore canonical order. Odd inversion count flips the coefficient; even inversion count preserves it, independent of the eventual metric factor.

slides.title: Outer Product Fast Path
slides.notes: Present the outer product as the cleanest basis-blade operation. A shared bit means the candidate spanning set repeats a basis vector, so the outer product is zero. With no shared bits, the output bitmap is just xor and the coefficient is only the input scales times the parity sign.

slides.title: Orthogonal Metric Factors
slides.notes: Connect the outer-product skeleton to the geometric product. In an orthogonal metric, repeated bits no longer force zero; they collapse into diagonal metric entries. This keeps the result as a single basis blade, which explains why diagonal Euclidean or mixed-signature tables are fast and compact.

slides.title: Tables Expose Product Contracts
slides.notes: Use the paired tables as a diagnostic lens rather than as memorization. The outer table has structural zeros wherever bitmasks overlap. The geometric-product table has the same sign convention but replaces duplicate factors by metric squares, so Euclidean repeated vectors behave like scalar one.

slides.title: Metric Products By Grade Selection
slides.notes: Explain scalar products, contractions, and commutators as reference operations built on top of the geometric product. The implementation can be optimized later, but grade selection gives a readable specification. If a faster contraction routine disagrees on these small basis-blade cases, the faster routine is suspect.

slides.title: Nonorthogonal Metrics Expand
slides.notes: This is the counterexample to any one-output-bitmap assumption. In a null or skew basis, a vector multiplication can produce an outer part and a contraction part at the same time. A product of two basis blades may therefore be a sparse dictionary, not a single weighted blade.

slides.title: Sparse Multivectors Distribute
slides.notes: Move from one blade pair to the sparse multivector layer. Each nonzero term of A multiplies each nonzero term of B, and equal output bitmaps must be merged. This is intentionally direct: it is slow enough to optimize later but transparent enough to trust as a reference.

slides.title: Unary Signs Are Grade Tables
slides.notes: Point out how much implementation work disappears once grade is a popcount. Reversion, grade involution, and Clifford conjugation do not inspect the individual basis-vector indices; they use periodic grade-dependent signs. These tiny tables are excellent smoke tests for off-by-one and integer-width mistakes.

slides.title: Operation Diagnostics
slides.notes: Turn the final slide sequence into a debugging checklist for a geometric algebra library. Every product routine should be checked against bit order, parity, duplicate handling, metric path, grade projection, coefficient cleanup, and associativity on a small table before it is trusted inside larger geometric algorithms.

slides.title: Carry Forward
slides.notes: Close by linking the assigned source page to the notebook. The source page frames later linear products as either matrix actions or sparse distributions over basis blades. Chapter 19 supplies the second route's foundation: reliable addresses, signs, metric factors, sparse merging, and diagnostic checks.
